statement: Prove that a space is T1 if and only if every singleton is closed.
solution: T1 means for any two distinct points each has a neighborhood excluding the other. If singletons are closed, then for x≠y, X\{y} is an open nbhd of x missing y. Conversely if T1 holds, for each x and any y≠x pick an open U_y∋y missing x; then X\{x}=∪U_y is open, so {x} is closed.

statement: Prove that every Hausdorff space is T1.
solution: Given x≠y, Hausdorff gives disjoint opens U∋x, V∋y. In particular U is a neighborhood of x missing y and V a neighborhood of y missing x, which is exactly the T1 condition.

statement: Prove that a subspace of a Hausdorff space is Hausdorff.
solution: Let A⊆X with X Hausdorff, and take distinct a,b∈A. There are disjoint opens U∋a, V∋b in X. Then A∩U and A∩V are disjoint opens in A separating a and b. So A is Hausdorff.

statement: Prove that a subspace of a regular space is regular.
solution: Let A⊆X, X regular. Take a∈A and a closed-in-A set C not containing a; write C=A∩D with D closed in X, so a∉D. Regularity of X gives disjoint opens U∋a, V⊇D. Then A∩U and A∩V are disjoint opens in A separating a from C. Hence A is regular. (Uses that A is T1 as a subspace of a T1 space.)

statement: Prove that the product of two Hausdorff spaces is Hausdorff.
solution: Let (x1,y1)≠(x2,y2) in X×Y; they differ in some coordinate, say x1≠x2. Hausdorffness of X gives disjoint opens U1∋x1, U2∋x2; then U1×Y and U2×Y are disjoint opens separating the two points in X×Y.

statement: Prove that every metric space is normal.
solution: For disjoint closed sets A,B in a metric space, the function f(x)=d(x,A)/(d(x,A)+d(x,B)) is continuous, 0 on A, 1 on B. Then f^{-1}([0,1/2)) and f^{-1}((1/2,1]) are disjoint open sets containing A and B respectively. Hence the space is normal.

statement: Prove that every compact Hausdorff space is normal.
solution: In compact Hausdorff X, disjoint closed sets are compact (closed in compact). Two disjoint compact sets in a Hausdorff space can be separated by disjoint open sets (see the compact-Hausdorff separation argument). Hence X is normal.

statement: Prove that a closed subspace of a normal space is normal.
solution: Let F⊆X closed, X normal. Sets closed in F are closed in X (F closed). Two disjoint F-closed sets are thus disjoint X-closed sets, separated by disjoint opens U,V in X; then F∩U, F∩V separate them in F. So F is normal.

statement: Prove that every second-countable space is separable.
solution: Let {B_n} be a countable basis (with each B_n nonempty). Pick x_n∈B_n; the set D={x_n} is countable. Any nonempty open U contains some B_n, hence x_n∈D, so U∩D≠∅. Thus D is dense and X is separable.

statement: Prove that every second-countable space is first countable.
solution: Let {B_n} be a countable basis. For a point x, the subfamily {B_n : x∈B_n} is countable and is a neighborhood basis at x: any open U∋x contains some basis element B_n with x∈B_n⊆U. Hence X is first countable.

statement: Prove that every second-countable space is Lindelof.
solution: Let {B_n} be a countable basis and {U_i} an open cover. Each U_i is a union of basis elements; let S be the set of indices n such that B_n⊆some U_i. Then {B_n : n∈S} covers X, is countable, and for each such n choose one U_{i(n)}⊇B_n. The countable family {U_{i(n)}} covers X. Hence X is Lindelof.

statement: Prove that a subspace of a second-countable space is second countable.
solution: If {B_n} is a countable basis for X and A⊆X, then {A∩B_n} is a countable collection of open sets in A. Given V open in A, V=A∩U with U open in X; U is a union of basis elements B_n⊆U, so V is the union of the corresponding A∩B_n. Hence {A∩B_n} is a countable basis for A.

statement: Prove that R with the standard topology is second countable.
solution: The open intervals with rational endpoints form a countable collection (indexed by pairs of rationals) and are a basis for the standard topology (b20). Hence R is second countable.

statement: Prove that in a Hausdorff space a sequence converges to at most one point.
solution: Suppose x_n→a and x_n→b with a≠b. Take disjoint opens U∋a, V∋b. Eventually all x_n∈U (convergence to a) and eventually all x_n∈V (to b), so some x_n∈U∩V=∅, a contradiction. Hence limits are unique.

statement: Prove that in a first-countable space, x is in the closure of A if and only if some sequence in A converges to x.
solution: If x_n∈A with x_n→x, every nbhd of x contains some x_n∈A, so x∈cl(A). Conversely if x∈cl(A), take a countable nested neighborhood basis B_1⊇B_2⊇... at x; each B_n meets A, pick x_n∈B_n∩A; then x_n→x since any nbhd of x contains some B_n.

statement: Prove that a discrete space is second countable if and only if it is countable.
solution: In the discrete topology every singleton is open, so any basis must contain each {x}; thus a basis has at least |X| elements. A countable basis forces X countable. Conversely if X is countable, the countable family of singletons {{x}} is a basis. Hence second countable iff countable.

statement: Prove that every regular space in which one-point sets are closed (a T3 space) is Hausdorff.
solution: A T3 space is regular and T1. In a T1 space points are closed (s01), so given distinct x,y the set {y} is closed and x∉{y}; regularity separates x from the closed set {y} by disjoint open sets, which is exactly the Hausdorff condition for x and y. Thus T3 ⇒ T2.

statement: State Urysohn's lemma and explain what it provides for a normal space.
solution: Urysohn's lemma: if X is normal and A,B are disjoint closed sets, then there is a continuous function f:X→[0,1] with f≡0 on A and f≡1 on B. It shows normal spaces have 'enough' continuous real-valued functions to separate disjoint closed sets, the key tool behind the Tietze extension theorem and the Urysohn metrization theorem.
